faq.q: Why is potassium sometimes omitted from the AG calculation?

faq.a: Albumin is an unmeasured anion; low albumin reduces the AG, so you add 2.5 mmol/L for each 1 g/dL drop below 4 g/dL.
faq.q: How does hypoalbuminemia affect the AG?

faq.a: Look for other high‑AG causes such as ketoacidosis, renal failure, or toxic ingestions and investigate accordingly.
faq.q: What is the next step if the AG is high but lactate is normal?

exam: A patient with severe malaria presents with a pH 7.25, HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L, Na⁺ 138 mmol/L, Cl⁻ 100 mmol/L. Calculate the AG and explain its significance — AG = 26 mmol/L, indicating high‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis likely from lactic acidosis; urgent fluid resuscitation and antimalarial therapy are needed.

You obtain a serum Na⁺ 140, K⁺ 4, Cl⁻ 105, HCO₃⁻ 14. The patient is a known diabetic with fruity breath. What does the AG tell you and what is your immediate management? — AG = 25 mmol/L, high‑AG metabolic acidosis from DKA; start insulin, fluids, and monitor potassium.

A patient with chronic kidney disease has Na⁺ 138, Cl⁻ 102, HCO₃⁻ 10, K⁺ 5.5. How do you interpret the AG and what are the treatment priorities? — AG = 26 mmol/L, high‑AG acidosis from uremia; consider dialysis if refractory, correct electrolytes, and manage volume status.

In a resource‑limited setting you lack a bicarbonate measurement. You have Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 108, and a bedside venous blood gas showing pH 7.30. How can you estimate the AG? — Approximate HCO₃⁻ from the Henderson‑Hasselbalch equation using pH and pCO₂, then calculate AG; a high estimate still points to high‑AG acidosis.

A patient on high‑dose IV saline develops a pH 7.28, HCO₃⁻ 16, Cl⁻ 115. Why is the AG normal and what does this indicate? — AG ≈ 9 mmol/L (normal); the acidosis is hyperchloremic from saline overload, treat by reducing chloride load.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with abdominal pain, vomiting, and a pH 7.20, HCO₃⁻ 9, Na⁺ 136, Cl⁻ 100. What is the likely cause of the high AG and next step? — Likely lactic acidosis from vaso‑occlusive crisis; give analgesia, hydration, and treat any infection.

You suspect ethylene glycol poisoning. Which lab findings support this and how does the AG help? — Very high AG (>30 mmol/L) with normal Cl⁻, low HCO₃⁻, and elevated osmolar gap; start fomepizole and consider dialysis.

A patient with severe diarrhoea has pH 7.32, HCO₃⁻ 18, Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 110. Explain the AG result and management. — AG ≈ 12 mmol/L (normal); this is a non‑anion‑gap metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss; replace fluids with balanced solutions and treat the diarrhoea.
ai.title: Calculating the Anion Gap
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The anion gap helps identify metabolic acidosis causes by comparing measured cations and anions. It is calculated from basic chemistry labs, often available even in low‑resource settings.

b: High AG indicates accumulation of acids (e.g., ketoacidosis, lactate).
Low/normal AG suggests hyperchloremic (non‑anion gap) acidosis.
sections.p: The anion gap (AG) is the difference between the primary measured cations (Na⁺) and the primary measured anions (Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻) in serum. It reflects unmeasured anions that accumulate in metabolic acidosis.

b: Formula without K⁺: AG = Na⁺ – (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻).
Formula with K⁺: AG = Na⁺ + K⁺ – (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻).
Albumin correction: for each 1 g/dL decrease below 4 g/dL, add 2.5 mmol/L to the AG.
sections.p: Calculate AG using the formula appropriate to the available labs. Adjust for albumin if hypoalbuminemia is present, as albumin contributes to the gap.

b: MUDPILES mnemonic (Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Isoniazid/Iron, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates).
Common local causes: severe malaria (lactic acidosis), diabetic ketoacidosis, renal failure, sepsis, toxic ingestions (e.g., ethylene glycol from adulterated alcohol).
sections.p: A high AG metabolic acidosis narrows the differential to a few common causes, many of which are prevalent in East Africa and other low‑resource settings.

b: Always state whether K⁺ was included.
Mention albumin correction when hypoalbuminemia is evident.
Link AG result to the next immediate management step.

t.a: Serum electrolytes (Na⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻, optionally K⁺)
t.b: Provides values needed to calculate the AG; a high AG points to an anion‑gap metabolic acidosis.
Allows correction of AG for hypoalbuminemia; low albumin can mask a high AG.
Distinguishes lactic acidosis as a cause of high AG.

b: Severe DKA: IV insulin, fluid resuscitation, potassium replacement after insulin started.
Lactic acidosis from sepsis/malaria: aggressive fluid resuscitation, treat infection (antibiotics, antimalarials).
Renal failure: dialysis if uremic acidosis is severe and refractory.
Toxin ingestion: specific antidotes (e.g., fomepizole for ethylene glycol) and hemodialysis if indicated.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; supportive measures address the acidosis while specific therapy is initiated.

b: Caused by diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis, saline overload.
sections.p: Non‑anion‑gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis, which has a normal AG but low HCO₃⁻ and high Cl⁻.

b: Always correct AG for albumin when <4 g/dL.
Check for sample hemolysis or improper handling.
sections.p: Low albumin, hypermagnesemia, or lab errors can give a falsely low AG.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe metabolic acidosis with pH < 7.1, altered mental status, or hemodynamic instability.
Rapidly rising lactate (>4 mmol/L) despite therapy.
Suspected toxic ingestion with high AG.
